query: For additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components, what single intervention could improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the current fabrication baseline, defines the processing and application conditions under which it should hold, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Preheating the build substrate and chamber during additive manufacturing of high-entropy alloys will reduce thermal gradients during solidification, thereby improving dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while minimizing fabrication-induced defects.
generation.material_initial_state: AM high-entropy alloy components produced under conventional conditions exhibit significant residual stresses, dimensional inaccuracies, heterogeneous microstructures, and defects such as porosity and cracking.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled preheating protocol for the substrate and build chamber (e.g., maintaining temperatures around 350–450 °C) immediately prior to and during the deposition process.
generation.conditions: The effect is expected under inert gas (e.g., argon) atmospheres and for alloy systems typical of high-entropy formulations processed by powder bed fusion or directed energy deposition. The intervention is applied during the entire build process, with temperature settings optimized for the specific HEA composition.
generation.structural_mediator: The maintained elevated temperature reduces steep thermal gradients, leading to a more uniform solidification front and minimizing residual stresses and phase inconsistencies.
generation.mechanism: Preheating moderates rapid cooling, thereby reducing thermal contraction and associated distortions. This stabilization of the melt pool dynamics and the solidification process results in improved interlayer bonding, refined microstructure, and a reduction in fabrication‐induced defects.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the current fabrication baseline, it is predicted that there will be a measurable improvement in dimensional precision (e.g., reduction of geometric deviations by approximately 10–20%) and an enhancement in mechanical properties (e.g., tensile strength and fatigue life), along with a lower incidence of defects such as porosity and cracking.
generation.baseline: Conventional additive manufacturing process for HEAs without preheating, which suffers from high thermal gradients, high residual stresses, and consequent dimensional and structural anomalies.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for HEA compositions with similar melting ranges and thermal properties; substantially different alloys or processes with already minimal thermal gradients may not see comparable benefits.
generation.uncertainty: The precise temperature range for optimal improvement and the exact magnitude of the improvement in mechanical or dimensional properties is uncertain and may vary with the specific alloy system and machine parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two identical sets of HEA components using the same additive manufacturing process. One group is built under standard conditions, and the other with the preheating protocol applied. Post-build, measure dimensional accuracy, residual stress levels, microstructural homogeneity, and mechanical performance (e.g., tensile strength, fatigue life).
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) or similar techniques for residual stress assessment
Optical/electron microscopy for microstructure and defect analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the preheated group does not show a statistically significant improvement (e.g., >10% better dimensional and mechanical performance and a reduction in measurable defects) compared to the standard group, or if unexpected defects arise, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.
